花昌町.note: The site of the Shinsengumi’s last Kyoto barracks (also called Fudōdō-mura), near Samegai, Shichijō, and the Horikawa; no such place-name survives today. The source glosses the name kashō-chō.

堀川国広.note: A short-sword of the Kyoto smith Horikawa Kunihiro (c.1531–1614); Toshizō’s companion blade to the long Izumi-no-kami Kanesada (see ch12, ch17).

笠間喜十郎.note: An Echigo rōnin drawn into the ambush; he died of his wound days later, naming Itō as the man behind it.

ch35.anchor: one plank bridge, with neither railing nor handrail
ch35.note: The bridge at Nijō in those years crossed the Kamo in two spans, resting midstream on a nakasu, a grassy sandbar — the ‘Nijō Nakasu’ of the chapter title. The river has since been narrowed and embanked and the sandbar is gone; the modern Nijō-ōhashi is a single span.

Tenchū, ‘the chastisement of Heaven,’ was the slogan under which loyalist swordsmen in these years murdered officials, merchants, and rival activists, often pinning a placard on the body to justify the killing as a public execution rather than a private one. Kennosuke, below, boasts of just such a tally.

Konnyaku (konjac) is a firm, near-tasteless jelly made from the corm of the devil’s-tongue plant, about as bland a food as a Japanese kitchen offers. ‘A man who will take neither vinegar nor konjac’ is a proverb for one so contrary that nothing whatever will move him.

ch35.anchor: served, too, as a constable's informer
ch35.note: A meakashi: a commoner, very often a reformed gambler or ex-convict, employed off the books by the town constables as a thief-taker and informer. Yohei’s past explains why he can read Toshizō’s trade at a glance and why his blood is up.

Hitokiri, ‘man-cutter’: the era’s word for its political assassins, a handful of whom (Kirino among them, see ch34) became legends. Shichiri claims the title for himself; the boast of a private count of the dead was itself a mark of the type.

ch35.anchor: whipped a tasuki round to bind back his sleeves
ch35.note: A tasuki is a cord looped across the back and over both shoulders to gather the long kimono sleeves out of the way of the arms; a swordsman going into a fight tied one on, here improvised from the sageo, the cord that secures the scabbard at the belt.

ch35.anchor: exposed the head on a stake
ch35.note: Sarashi-kubi: the severed head set on a spike at a public place beside a written placard naming the dead man’s offense. It was the ordinary end the loyalist bands meted out to those they killed, and the fate Toshizō grants he himself only just escaped.

Daikon, the big white radish: as a term of contempt it means a duffer, a nobody — used of a wooden actor or, as here, of a swordsman reckoned no threat. Shichiri had sold Toshizō to his hirelings as an easy kill.
